craftinginfo-quenching-text:
Ferrous metal (iron, meteoric iron, and steel) tool and weapon heads can be hardened by quenching. Non-ferrous metals gain nothing.

Quenching
Quench with a layer of fire clay on the piece to improve its durability, or bare to improve its power. Heat the piece into the range shown in its tooltip, then toss it into water or rightmouse a water block or barrel of quenchant, and bring it below 100C quickly.
Each quench gives a larger bonus than the last, and every bonus counts toward the same running total whether you spend it on power or on durability.

Stress
Every quench also builds stress in the metal, and each piece has its own hidden tolerance. Most pieces take three or four quenches; a rare few take ten. Push a piece past its tolerance and it overstresses: it is not destroyed, but it loses most of the bonuses it had accumulated and will never take heat treatment again.
To judge how much a piece has left, strike it against an anvil and listen. Think of it as string tension: a fresh piece rings low and slack, and the note climbs as stress builds, until a piece close to its tolerance sings tight and high. An overstressed piece rings like a broken tuning fork.
item-handbooktext-clay-fire:
Fire clay is found naturally in areas of bauxite sand or gravel in small patches at the surface, and underlaying black and anthracite coal deposits in large patches, underground. It can also be crafted by combining red or blue clay with powdered flint.

Special Uses
Fireclay is also useful in quenching. Place a piece of fireclay in the crafting grid alongside a tool or weapon head that does not have a handle. This will cover it in a thin layer of clay, so that the next quench improves durability instead of power.
